occurrence.window: The IMO's Net-Zero Framework was approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025, but its formal adoption vote at the second Extraordinary Session (MEPC/ES.2, October 13-17, 2025) was itself postponed by a procedural vote (57 in favour of delay, 49 against, 21 abstaining) rather than adopted; adoption is now rescheduled to reconvene in fall 2026, one year later. Independently of that vote, Singapore's methanol-bunkering licenses (awarded to three suppliers) run 2026-01-01 to 2030-12-31 regardless of the framework's adoption status.
occurrence.label: The IMO's global shipping-fuel carbon framework is delayed a year, but methanol-bunkering infrastructure is being built on its own schedule

title: The IMO Net-Zero Framework vote keeps slipping; the methanol-bunkering buildout it was supposed to trigger is already running on a separate clock
short_title: IMO Net-Zero vote and methanol bunkering
thesis: The IMO's Net-Zero Framework, a mandatory marine-fuel standard and the first global carbon-pricing scheme for international shipping, covering ocean-going ships over 5,000 gross tonnage that emit 85% of international shipping's CO2, was approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 but its formal adoption vote was itself postponed at the October 2025 extraordinary session by a 57-49-21 procedural vote after sustained US pressure, and is not scheduled to reconvene until fall 2026. General coverage of this correctly runs it as a story about the framework's political fragility and whether it survives at all. What that coverage misses is that the fuel-supply side of the transition it was meant to force is not waiting for the vote: Singapore, the world's largest bunkering port, has already awarded five-year methanol-bunkering licenses (2026-01-01 to 2030-12-31) to three suppliers selected from 13 applicants, and green methanol already leads today's alternative-fuel adoption with 112+ methanol-capable ships in commercial operation. The buildout, bunkering terminals, methanol production and supply contracts, ship-owner fuel commitments, is proceeding on ship-owner and port-authority decisions made independently of whether IMO's carbon price is ever formally adopted, which is the opposite of how the story is being told.
why_now: Two dated facts sit on top of each other and are not connected anywhere found this run: the framework's own adoption clock was just reset (delayed exactly one year, from October 2025 to fall 2026, by a formal vote with a recorded count), while the physical fuel-supply infrastructure clock was not reset at all (Singapore's licenses took effect 2026-01-01 on their own five-year schedule, unaffected by the IMO vote). That divergence is the whole finding: coverage treats the vote as the pacing item for the entire energy transition in shipping, when the commercial fuel-supply side is already committed on a schedule that runs through 2030 regardless of the vote's outcome.
retail_gap: Maritime and policy trade press covers the IMO vote in detail (the procedural postponement, the US pressure campaign, the 57-49-21 count) and separately covers Singapore's bunkering-license awards as a shipping-industry item. No source found this run puts the two together as a single mispriced fact: that the fuel transition's investable infrastructure, bunkering terminals, methanol supply contracts, is being built and licensed on a fixed multi-year schedule that does not depend on the IMO vote's success or failure, meaning the framework's political fragility says less about the pace of real capital deployment in marine alternative fuels than the headline coverage implies.

unmappedness.rationale: Scored at 64 rather than higher because both halves of the fact pattern, the IMO vote's postponement and Singapore's license award, are individually well covered in trade press; this is a joining problem, not a discovery of an unreported event. Held above 60 because no source found this run states the joining fact directly (that the bunkering buildout is running on a schedule independent of the vote), and because the specific listed suppliers, storage-terminal operators, and shipowner counterparties behind the Singapore licenses and the 112+ methanol-capable-ship fleet are not named or scored anywhere found this run. A chain build would need to establish which of the three Singapore-licensed suppliers, and which vessel owners committed to methanol newbuilds, are public and reachable.

evidence.claim: In October 2025, negotiations at the second extraordinary session of the IMO's Marine Environment Protection Committee ended with a decision to delay the vote on the adoption of the Net-Zero Framework by one year; the session is set to reconvene in the fall of 2026, prolonging policy uncertainty around the transition to zero-emission shipping.
evidence.source_name: Global Maritime Forum, A guide to the IMO's Net-Zero Framework
source_excerpt: In October 2025, negotiations at the second extraordinary session of the International Maritime Organization's Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) ended with a decision to delay the vote on the adoption of the Net-Zero Framework by one year.
The session is set to reconvene in the fall of 2026, prolonging policy uncertainty around the transition to zero-emission shipping.

evidence.claim: The motion to postpone adoption of the IMO Net-Zero Framework passed with 57 votes in favour, 49 against and 21 abstaining.
evidence.source_name: Hill Dickinson, IMO's Net-Zero Framework: Adoption adjourned, and consensus building continues
evidence.source_excerpt: The motion passed with 57 votes in favour, 49 against and 21 abstaining.

evidence.claim: The IMO Net-Zero Framework sets a global fuel standard and emission pricing scheme applying to large ocean-going ships over 5,000 gross tonnage, which emit 85% of the total CO2 emissions from international shipping.
evidence.source_name: Ammonia Energy Association, The IMO approved its Net-zero Framework. Now what?
source_excerpt: a global fuel standard and emission pricing scheme designed to drive the decarbonization of the maritime sector
large ocean-going ships over 5,000 gross tonnage, which emit 85% of the total CO2 emissions from international shipping

evidence.claim: Singapore's Maritime and Port Authority will award methanol-bunkering licenses to Global Energy Trading Pte Ltd, Golden Island Pte Ltd, and PetroChina International (Singapore) Pte Ltd, selected from a total of 13 applicants, valid for a five-year period from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2030.
evidence.source_name: Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore, Singapore to Award Licences for Methanol Bunkering
source_excerpt: Licences will be awarded to Global Energy Trading Pte Ltd, Golden Island Pte Ltd, and PetroChina International (Singapore) Pte Ltd
The three companies were selected from a total of 13 applicants through a comprehensive evaluation process
